query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings is predominantly governed by the formation of a thin, adherent, and self-healing oxide layer (largely derived from the Cr and Fe components) that reduces friction and abrasion during wear. In other words, the in‐situ oxidation at elevated temperatures modifies the surface into a protective scale that mediates wear behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, equimolar, nanocrystalline thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate with no intentional pre-oxidation (i.e., in its unoxidized state).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment in an oxygen-rich environment (e.g., hold at ~400°C for a fixed time) to intentionally develop a uniform and adherent oxide scale prior to wear testing, compared to the as-deposited baseline.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted at high temperatures (approximately 300–500°C) under moderate-to-high mechanical loading conditions in an atmosphere that allows oxidation, to simulate service conditions for high-temperature protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, continuous, and adherent oxide scale (primarily Cr- and Fe-based oxides) on the coating surface that acts as a diffusion barrier and reduces metal-to-metal contact during wear.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the thermally activated oxidation of surface species in the FeNiCrCoCu coating leads to the in-situ formation of a protective oxide layer. This oxide layer lowers the local coefficient of friction and effectively reduces abrasive wear by cushioning the contact and preventing direct exposure of the underlying metal. The self-healing nature of the oxide, if continuously regenerated under operating conditions, sustains the wear performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that are pre-oxidized (and thus develop the protective oxide layer) will exhibit significantly lower wear rates and friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings when tested under identical high-temperature wear conditions. Microscopy and diffraction analyses should reveal a continuous, low-porosity oxide scale on the surface of the improved samples.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating with its native microstructure and no intentional oxide build-up.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature (300–500°C) wear conditions in oxygen-containing environments. At room temperature or in non-oxidative atmospheres, the role of oxide formation may be minimal, limiting the applicability of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, phase distribution, and thickness of the oxide scale, as well as the detailed kinetics of its formation and self-healing behavior, remain uncertain and may depend strongly on processing parameters and the specific environmental oxygen partial pressure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on an identical substrate. Subject one set to a controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment (e.g., heat at 400°C in air for a predetermined duration) to deliberately form an oxide layer, while keeping the other set as-deposited. Conduct identical high-temperature wear tests (under defined load and temperature in an oxidizing atmosphere) on both sets.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) during wear testing
Wear rate (e.g., via weight loss and/or profilometry)
Surface morphology and integrity of the oxide scale (using SEM/EDS)
Phase identification of the surface layer (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and COF compared to the as-deposited samples, or if the oxide scale either does not form or degrades rapidly without providing any observable protective effect, then the hypothesis that a protective oxide scale governs high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution.
